top_three.article_content_en:
Michael Burry says Anthropic's IPO filing this week has reinforced his concerns that the entire AI ecosystem is at risk of disaster. The investor of "The Big Short" fame wrote in a Substack post on Tuesday that the first in-depth look at Claude's parent company, ahead of what could be the biggest IPO in history, threw up a bunch of red flags.

Burry pointed to Anthropic's huge spending commitments, slowing revenue, and tangled ties. He said that Anthropic has struck deals to buy about $537 billion of compute from the likes of Amazon, Alphabet, and Microsoft, and reached preliminary agreements worth hundreds of billions more with others such as SpaceXAI, putting its total commitments at about 12 times its current annual run-rate revenue.

"This is not stated clearly in the S-1, and in my view it is the most deserved headline from it," Burry wrote in a Tuesday Substack post. He underscored how hyperscalers like Amazon and Alphabet act as Anthropic's "lenders, vendors, channel providers, and shareholders." He also outlined its deal with Broadcom, which involves Apollo and Blackstone and includes convertible notes and structured credit tranches.

"Just remember, the reason this is so complex is because too much debt is needed, and it must be unloaded from the balance sheets of those involved," Burry wrote. "While some may see all the circularity and connectedness as security on the way up, and that is not wrong, it does leave the entire organism catastrophically vulnerable either on a pause or on the way down," he added.

He also described financing arrangements in the AI space as "garish and audacious," and said hyperscalers aren't generating enough cash to fund the AI buildout so they're resorting to "Byzantine" deals. Burry said it was a "very similar" situation with vendor financing during the dot-com bubble, saying "people keep making the same mistakes with every new thing." In its filing, Anthropic said its revenue surpassed $16 billion for the first six months of this year, a 14-fold increase from the first half of 2025.

Its operating loss narrowed by about two-thirds to below $700 million, and it generated nearly $4 billion in operating cash flow. Burry initially commented on Anthropic's filing in a Substack chat thread on Monday. He said that revenue was "slowing," citing Anthropic's claim that third-quarter revenue was 86 times the $197 million it generated in the fourth quarter of 2024, or about $16.9 billion.

That would mean Anthropic's revenue grew by about 46% between the second and third quarters of this year, after soaring 144% between the first and second quarters. "Overall slowing of growth is not attributed to a decline in tokenmaxxing, but I did not expect that to be mentioned," Burry wrote.

Burry was referring to the trend of maximizing AI token consumption, which has fallen out of favor in recent months given its costs. In another comment, Burry wrote that large language models (LLMs) like Claude are "improving" and "already being used more efficiently and that trend will continue, to the detriment of their growth rate." Burry said he's focused on the complexity and fragility of the debt financing many AI deals, hurdles to installing new graphics chips shoring up demand for older chips, a potential crash in memory chip prices once the shortage eases, compression and small language models (SLMs) reducing the need for computing power, and the "fundamentals behind not just companies but the deals they are doing." Responding to a subscriber who said that Big Tech companies are shifting from Anthropic's AI models to their own, and that tokens are rapidly being commoditized, Burry wrote: "Yes, that is what I hear." Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Burry's posts.

The contrarian investor shot to fame after his massive wager against the mid-2000s housing bubble was chronicled in the book and movie "The Big Short." He pivoted from running a hedge fund to writing about his personal investments on Substack last winter. A recurring theme of his work since then has been deep skepticism of the AI boom.

He's flagged slowing growth, overinvestment in microchips and data centers, aggressive accounting, hidden liabilities, and circular financing deals.

"While some may see all the circularity and connectedness as security on the way up, and that is not wrong, it does leave the entire organism catastrophically vulnerable either on a pause or on the way down," he added.

Burry said it was a "very similar" situation with vendor financing during the dot-com bubble, saying "people keep making the same mistakes with every new thing." In its filing, Anthropic said its revenue surpassed $16 billion for the first six months of this year, a 14-fold increase from the first half of 2025.

Its operating loss narrowed by about two-thirds to below $700 million, and it generated nearly $4 billion in operating cash flow. Burry initially commented on Anthropic's filing in a Substack chat thread on Monday. He said that revenue was "slowing," citing Anthropic's claim that third-quarter revenue was 86 times the $197 million it generated in the fourth quarter of 2024, or about $16.9 billion.

That would mean Anthropic's revenue grew by about 46% between the second and third quarters of this year, after soaring 144% between the first and second quarters. "Overall slowing of growth is not attributed to a decline in tokenmaxxing, but I did not expect that to be mentioned," Burry wrote.

Burry was referring to the trend of maximizing AI token consumption, which has fallen out of favor in recent months given its costs. In another comment, Burry wrote that large language models (LLMs) like Claude are "improving" and "already being used more efficiently and that trend will continue, to the detriment of their growth rate." Burry said he's focused on the complexity and fragility of the debt financing many AI deals, hurdles to installing new graphics chips shoring up demand for older chips, a potential crash in memory chip prices once the shortage eases, compression and small language models (SLMs) reducing the need for computing power, and the "fundamentals behind not just companies but the deals they are doing." Responding to a subscriber who said that Big Tech companies are shifting from Anthropic's AI models to their own, and that tokens are rapidly being commoditized, Burry wrote: "Yes, that is what I hear." Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Burry's posts.

The contrarian investor shot to fame after his massive wager against the mid-2000s housing bubble was chronicled in the book and movie "The Big Short." He pivoted from running a hedge fund to writing about his personal investments on Substack last winter. A recurring theme of his work since then has been deep skepticism of the AI boom.
He's flagged slowing growth, overinvestment in microchips and data centers, aggressive accounting, hidden liabilities, and circular financing deals.

fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】投资人迈克尔·伯里（Michael Burry）；Anthropic公司；亚马逊、谷歌、微软（云厂商/股东）：揭露Anthropic高达5370亿美元的算力债务 commitments，抨击超大规模云厂商构筑的“出借人、供应商与股东”三位一体闭环模式
【起因与机理】质疑当前AI基础设施融资依赖高杠杆债务，类比互联网泡沫时期的厂商融资模式，认为整体系统缺乏现金流支撑
【关键数据与实测】披露Anthropic与云巨头绑定高达5370亿美元的算力采购债务，杠杆倍数远超其营收能力。

fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Michael Burry (Investor); Anthropic; Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft (Hyperscalers) (Anthropic S-1 IPO Filing): Exposed $537 billion in compute debt commitments; criticized the circular 'lender-vendor-shareholder' ecosystem
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Concerns over high-leverage financing models reminiscent of dot-com era vendor financing, lacking sustainable cash flow

Artificial intelligence is not causing the disruptions but identifying gaps that are difficult to fix.

Banks such as JP Morgan Chase blamed software-related bugs for the service issues. (Charles Krupa/AP)

Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency have told members of Congress that this week’s widespread tech outages were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities identified by artificial intelligence, according to three sources familiar with the private conversations.

Over the la
top_three.summary_en: Wall Street executives and the NSA confirmed to Congress that recent nationwide tech outages were not cyberattacks, but resulted from legacy systems being overwhelmed by emergency patches triggered by AI-identified vulnerabilities. This highlights the fragility of aging IT infrastructure when subjected to the high-frequency deployment demands of automated security remediation.
top_three.title_zh: AI诱发补丁潮致美全境关键基础设施瘫痪
top_three.summary_zh: 华尔街银行与美国国家安全局在国会闭门听证中披露，近期美境内大规模断网系由AI识别漏洞后引发的紧急修补程序导致系统负载过载所致
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】摩根大通（JP Morgan Chase）、美国国家安全局（NSA）、国土安全部部长马克韦恩·穆林（Markwayne Mullin）在美国国会闭门听证会：由AI识别出的安全漏洞引发紧急补丁大规模排队更新，最终导致金融、航空及情报通讯系统崩溃
【起因与机理】AI模型在内网安全审计中识别出大量漏洞，企业与机构因担忧黑客利用同类工具发起攻击，从而被迫进行高频、激进的补丁更新
【核心事实细节】核心起因：由AI识别漏洞驱动的高频紧急补丁过载，导致金融、航空与情报系统崩溃。
【涉及范围与推进】行业后续：迫使关键基础设施运营商重新评估系统冗余设计，以应对AI加剧的安全修补压力。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] JP Morgan Chase, NSA, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin (Congressional private hearings): Massive system failures across financial, aviation, and intelligence networks caused by overwhelming software patching queues triggered by AI-detected vulnerabilities
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Urgency to patch vulnerabilities identified by AI to preempt malicious actors using similar tools against legacy infrastructure
[Regulatory & Investigation Focus] Root cause: Overload caused by high-frequency emergency patching triggered by AI-detected vulnerabilities.
[Official Stance & Demand] Outlook: Urgency for operators of critical infrastructure to re-engineer system resilience to accommodate AI-augmented security demands.

top_three.title: FAA pauses installations of Juniper routers like the one officials believe contributed to Friday's nationwide ground stop; HPE says its device wasn't defective (Neil Vigdor/New York Times)
top_three.title_en: FAA pauses installations of Juniper routers like the one officials believe contributed to Friday's nationwide ground stop; HPE says its device wasn't defective (Neil Vigdor/New York Times)
top_three.author: New York Times
top_three.content_snippet: Federal officials said they believed that a router made by Juniper Networks caused a data overload that disrupted communications.
top_three.summary_en: The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has suspended the installation and operation of Juniper Networks routers, following findings that a recently installed unit in El Dorado, Arkansas, contributed to last week's nationwide air traffic control ground stop. Despite Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) asserting no defects, the incident, coupled with recent outages at the National Security Agency's classified communications network, highlights mounting concerns over the resilience of critical infrastructure supply chains and maintenance protocols.
top_three.article_content_en:
The Federal Aviation Administration has paused the installation of the routers that were linked to last week’s national ground stop and turned off any Juniper routers that were already installed. Technicians linked Friday’s disruption of key air traffic control systems to one of these routers that had just been installed. A network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline Tuesday after what one U.S. official described as “routine maintenance.” Meanwhile, President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday. He is scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.

President Donald Trump and Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul shows the documents during a signing ceremony in Manila, Philippines, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026.

As of Tuesday, the Federal Aviation Administration has paused the installation of the routers that were linked to last week’s national ground stop and turned off any Juniper routers that were already installed. The decision was made after technicians linked Friday’s disruption of key air traffic control systems to one of these routers that had just been installed in El Dorado, Arkansas.

A network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline Tuesday after what one U.S. official described as “routine maintenance.” Another official clarified that “mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational.” The NSA episode is the latest in a recent series of cyber-related disruptions to critical government and private sector functions.

President Donald Trumparrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.

Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump’s first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un.

Jay Clayton, the Trump administration’s director of national intelligence, says the recent spate of cyber disruptions aren’t a result of attacks or nefarious acts.

Instead, Clayton said, the outages appear to be because many government institutions and private companies are upgrading their computer systems at around the same time.

Clayton offered the explanation in interviews on CNBC and Fox Business.

He spoke hours after it was revealed that a classified internal National Security Agency network was offline as a result after what the agency said was “routine maintenance.”

After pitching skeptical Republican senators on a $50 billion funding request for the nation’s air transportation system, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy expressed openness to other options. That could include Congress breaking up the request into pieces, with the initial focus on the most critical needs for air safety.

“I would hope that they don’t do that to me, but I’ll take what I can get,” Duffy told reporters after the meeting with GOP senators.

Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to modernize key infrastructure for air travel. Duffy said all of that money has been “set aside,” requiring lawmakers to approve additional funding.

He acknowledged the breadth of the request, which has spurred pushback from some Republicans who have expressed concern that it goes beyond core safety needs.

“I wanted to put everything on the table,” Duffy said. “I wanted to show it all to them. I know the Congress will … pressure test it, look at it and they’ll make a determination.”

The State Department has announced a new overhaul of its arms sales approval process for closely allied foreign governments.

In upcoming changes to the International Arms Trafficking Regulations, the department said Tuesday it would remove items from the U.S. Munitions List that do not provide “a critical military or intelligence advantage” to the purchaser. This will largely affect so-called “dual-use items” that can have both civilian and military functions.

In addition, the department, which is in charge of approving foreign arms sales, said it would create a general license category that will pro-approve the sale of certain materiel to “most trusted partner governments.” It will also adopt a presumption of approval for some requests that must still go through the vetting process, it said.

The changes are the latest modifications to the arms sale approval process that the Trump administration has sought to speed up to benefit both American defense contractors and allied countries.

Several Republican senators are voicing skepticism about a $50 billion request from the Trump administration for the nation’s air transportation system.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related,” said Sen. Ted Cruz, chairman of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, & Transportation, which has jurisdiction over air safety issues.

“We’re not going to give them $50 billion,” said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La. “But I think that we are willing to provide the money to replace the copper wires with fiber optics, and to try to stop the bleeding.

The lawmakers’ comments came after a closed-door meeting with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. The administration formally requested a $50 billion investment Tuesday to boost airline safety and the nation’s airports. The request came after the longest air traffic ground stop in 25 years.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said he understands the need for upgrades, but doesn’t believe taxpayers should have to pay for them.

“I don’t understand why the airline industry is not paying for this,” Scott said.

“We are making rare earth at a level that we’ve never made before,” Trump said in Manila when appearing with leaders from Japan, India and Australia, a grouping known as the Quad to counter China’s influence in the region.

“Everything that we need, we’ll have in 10 months,” Trump said. “We’re producing major numbers when it comes to rare earth.”

Experts in the industry believe it will take years.

China has used its near-monopoly in rare earth minerals processing to force a trade truce with the U.S. in 2025. Since then, the Trump administration has invested domestically and forged partnerships to rebuild the country’s rare earth elements supply chain.

A U.S. fighter jet has carried out a strike on a missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz belonging to Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, a U.S. official says.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military operations, says “precision munitions” were used in the strike on Qeshm Island and that the U.S. was responding to “aggression” toward U.S. personnel.

The U.S. military has periodically carried out what appear to be limited strikes on Qeshm Island and other Iranian targets this month.

A network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what one U.S. official described as “routine maintenance.”

A defense official said Tuesday that the problem affected NSANet, a classified internal network. A U.S. official said that the NSA “experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance” and that though “while some internal systems were affected, mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues.” Another person familiar with the matter said the issue occurred during routine patching.

The three individuals spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss non-public information.

The NSA episode is the latest in a series of cyber-related disruptions to critical government and private sector functions, including one Friday that resulted in a ground stop of air traffic in the United States, and a technical issue that affected the banking industry on Monday.

The Federal Aviation Administration has paused the installation of the routers that were linked to last week’s national ground stop, and turned off any Juniper routers that were already installed.

The decision was made after technicians linked Friday’s disruption of key air traffic control systems to one of these routers that had just been installed in El Dorado, Arkansas.

For now, the FAA is relying on older Cisco routers that have been in place for 25 years to continue operating the network while they investigate the cause of Friday’s problems at 17 of the nation’s 22 regional air traffic control centers.

The routers that malfunctioned last week are being tested in a lab at the headquarters of the company that installed them named L3Harris.

The top-finishing Republican in Alaska’s gubernatorial race praised as a statesman the Democrat who dropped out of the race to support a fellow Democrat.

Republican Bernadette Wilson, endorsed by Trump, had urged the other two Republicans in the race to withdraw after the open primary to create a clearer lane for her against Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins in the Nov. 3 ranked vote general election, which Kreiss-Tomkins won.

The two Republicans, a former mayor and a former state attorney general, stayed in the race, highlighting differences in experience and priorities with the business owner Wilson. They urged voters to rank the GOP candidates, calling that an important strategy.

After advancing from the August primary, Democrat Tom Begich withdrew and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins. His campaign said it was the best way to bring Democratic donors and voters together.

Wilson said Begich’s decision showed a willingness “to put pride and ego aside.”

Jeffries said they talked about disaster assistance and also priorities for health care and lowering the high costs of living.

“We’re committed to making sure that we deliver disaster relief to the people of Altadena and the Pacific Palisades,” he said, calling it unacceptable that those communities have gone without aid nearly two years after the devastating wildfires.

He said he also thanked Gov. Gavin Newsom for his leadership around the state’s response to nationwide Republican redistricting efforts.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said he spoke to Duffy on Sunday but there are still more questions and answers about the airline disruptions.

Taken together with other recent outages, he said it’s unclear if it’s infrastructure related or whether there’s “malignant activity.”

He mentioned the Microsoft email outage, the FAA ground stops and reports of problems at the NSA.

“I think it’s time for the administration to come up to the Hill and explain themselves,” he said, “so we can be informed about the steps that need to be taken.”

He panned the administration’s request for $50 billion to modernize the air traffic control system as Congress assesses the situation.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is pitching to lawmakers the Trump administration’s request for $50 billion to fully modernize the nation’s air traffic control system.

Duffy said there has been a historic underinvestment in aviation. And now lawmakers have a choice.

“They have to make a decision. What do they want to do? Everything? Or do they want to give me some piecemeal?” Duffy said. “ I hope they don’t piecemeal it. There’s been too much piecemeal happening over the course over 20 or 30 years. I hope we get the full investment.”

Duffy’s comments came as he prepared to meet with GOP senators Tuesday on Capitol Hill. Earlier in the day, the administration made a formal request for the funding and detailed where it hopes to invest the money. The beefed-up request comes after the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.

The Senate committee hearing to consider Acting Navy Sec. Hung Cao for the permanent job wrapped up after 2.5 hours that focused largely on the Iran war’s costs and conditions aboard Navy ships supporting the war.

The hearing ended with a clash between Cao and Democratic New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand over sailors’ suicide attempts aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which supported the war during a record-breaking deployment.

Gillibrand targeted Cao’s assertions that reports of mental health concerns were dishonest. She also dismissed Cao’s use of the term “suicide mitigations” to describe suicide attempts.

Cao said a sailor who jumped off the Lincoln was not attempting suicide because he later admitted as much and was wearing a life preserver. Gillibrand pushed back: “What was he trying to do, swim to Guam?”

The Trump administration has nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to Chief of Staff of the Army — the top uniformed post in the service — after he stepped into the job for months following the unexplained firing of Gen. Randy George in April.

Adam Telle, the man currently serving as the acting Secretary of the Army following the departure of Dan Driscoll from the top civilian post in August, said that LaNeve “is the right leader at the right time to modernize the Army and ensure our Soldiers are prepared to dominate on any battlefield” in a post to social media.

LaNeve has seen a meteoric rise through the ranks since the start of the Trump administration. LaNeve was promoted to be Hegseth’s top military aide shortly after he arrived at the Pentagon and was suddenly nominated him to be the Army’s vice chief of staff last October even though there was an officer in the job at the time.

The Kentucky Republican congressman announced he’s running for Kentucky governor in 2027.

Comer said in an online town hall Monday night that serving Kentucky “is a calling for me.”

“With your support, we can restore hope and create growth all across Kentucky,” Comer said.

As head of the House Oversight Committee, he’s conducted extensive investigations of former President Joe Biden and his family as well as the Trump administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files.

Comer has served as Kentucky’s agriculture secretary and was also a state lawmaker.

Two Democrats have announced their campaigns for governor: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and Rocky Adkins, a former top adviser to Gov. Andy Beshear.

Beshear, who’s been mentioned as a potential presidential candidate, will leave office next year after serving two terms.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to fly to a college football game shortly after a nationwide ground stop which caused massive travel disruptions and left people stranded across the country.

Mullin, speaking on CNBC, acknowledged earlier reporting in the New York Post that he flew to the LSU-Texas college football game a day after all planes were grounded.

Mullin answered in the affirmative when asked whether he’s required to fly on government planes and that he paid for the trip personally.

“We would have never went if the airways weren’t completely open,” he said on CNBC. “They’d been completely open for 21 hours.”

He added: “We would have never taken airspace if airspace wasn’t open. And we still gotta live our lives at the same time.”

Hours before his flight, Mullin was at the White House alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy giving updates on the ground stop.

The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports.

Cao confirmed the figure during his Senate confirmation hearing Tuesday for the position of Navy secretary. He was being questioned by Democratic Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who cited reports on the blockade’s costs.

“That means the American taxpayers are spending about $1 billion a month just on this blockade,” Warren stated.

Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly asked Cao about the current conditions on the various destroyers that are deployed around the world, including reports of diminishing rations that have caused some sailors to lose an alarming amount of weight.

Cao responded, “Well, senator, it’s just not what they want. It’s like my kids opening up the refrigerator door and saying there’s nothing to eat in here.”

“Mr. Secretary, somebody doesn’t lose 45 pounds just because they don’t like the options. I don’t think that’s a fair assessment,” Kelly said.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren that he doesn’t know the cost of the damage to a U.S. Navy base in Bahrain that was struck by an Iranian attack. Cao previously told The Epoch Times that Iranian strikes “blew the hell out of” the installation.

Cao told Warren the Navy hasn’t been able to conduct a full damage assessment because it’s in a “nonpermissive area for us to go.” He did not confirm a Wall Street Journal report that estimated the cost to be $400 million. But Cao said he would find out the costs.

Warren noted that the base is home to U.S. Naval Forces Central Command and the 5th Fleet.

The Republican chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee has rejected Trump’s plan to return to the use of steam-powered catapults to launch jets off aircraft carriers.

“Returning to steam is a nonstarter, and everybody needs to understand that,” said Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi. Wicker was speaking to Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao during his nomination hearing to become Navy secretary.

Democrats have also expressed an aversion to returning to steam.

In August, Trump ordered the U.S. Navy to remove the advanced electromagnetic system used to launch fighter jets from its newest type of aircraft carrier and return to older steam catapults he has long said he prefers.

Trump’s mandate would likely cost billions of dollars and revert the Navy’s most advanced ships to a system that takes more sailors to operate and is more difficult to maintain.

linked_tweets.author: KevTheHermit
linked_tweets.content_zh: 对 CVE-2026-114938（又名 Java4Shell）进行功能利用 POC。这不是通用漏洞，需要针对特定​​应用程序，您需要具有 AVX-512 VBMI 支持的 CPU、易受攻击的 JDK 版本，并且应用程序需要使用 Base64，请注意 tomcats 基本身份验证和 java-jwt 提供预身份验证可利用路径。这次是 GLM5.3 运行我的代理而不是 Claude Code
linked_tweets.content_en: Have a functional exploit POC for CVE-2026-114938 aka Java4Shell. This is not a generic exploit and will need to be application specific, you need a CPU with AVX-512 VBMI support, vulnerable JDK Version, and the app needs to use Base64, note that tomcats basic auth and java-jwt provide pre-auth exploitable path. This time it was GLM5.3 was running my agents instead of Claude Code

news.title: Anthropic’s IPO Is Igniting a Massive AI Wealth Boom in San Francisco
news.title_en: Anthropic’s IPO Is Igniting a Massive AI Wealth Boom in San Francisco

inline_images.caption: Bloomberg/Getty Images Michael Burry, the investor of "The Big Short" fame.
inline_images.alt: Bloomberg/Getty Images Michael Burry, the investor of "The Big Short" fame.

news.author: Bloomberg
news.content_snippet:
Michael Burry says Anthropic's IPO filing this week has reinforced his concerns that the entire AI ecosystem is at risk of disaster. The investor of "The Big Short" fame wrote in a Substack post on Tuesday that the first in-depth look at Claude's parent company, ahead of what could be the biggest IPO in history, threw up a bunch of red flags.

news.summary_en: Investor Michael Burry, analyzing Anthropic's S-1 filing, identified $537 billion in compute procurement commitments to hyperscalers like Amazon, Alphabet, and Microsoft, representing 12 times its annual run-rate revenue. Burry warned that these complex financing loops, involving vendor financing and structured credit, create systemic fragility, suggesting that any deceleration in AI demand could trigger catastrophic debt defaults across the ecosystem.
news.article_content_en:
Michael Burry says Anthropic's IPO filing this week has reinforced his concerns that the entire AI ecosystem is at risk of disaster. The investor of "The Big Short" fame wrote in a Substack post on Tuesday that the first in-depth look at Claude's parent company, ahead of what could be the biggest IPO in history, threw up a bunch of red flags.

Burry pointed to Anthropic's huge spending commitments, slowing revenue, and tangled ties. He said that Anthropic has struck deals to buy about $537 billion of compute from the likes of Amazon, Alphabet, and Microsoft, and reached preliminary agreements worth hundreds of billions more with others such as SpaceXAI, putting its total commitments at about 12 times its current annual run-rate revenue.

"This is not stated clearly in the S-1, and in my view it is the most deserved headline from it," Burry wrote in a Tuesday Substack post. He underscored how hyperscalers like Amazon and Alphabet act as Anthropic's "lenders, vendors, channel providers, and shareholders." He also outlined its deal with Broadcom, which involves Apollo and Blackstone and includes convertible notes and structured credit tranches.

"Just remember, the reason this is so complex is because too much debt is needed, and it must be unloaded from the balance sheets of those involved," Burry wrote. "While some may see all the circularity and connectedness as security on the way up, and that is not wrong, it does leave the entire organism catastrophically vulnerable either on a pause or on the way down," he added.

He also described financing arrangements in the AI space as "garish and audacious," and said hyperscalers aren't generating enough cash to fund the AI buildout so they're resorting to "Byzantine" deals. Burry said it was a "very similar" situation with vendor financing during the dot-com bubble, saying "people keep making the same mistakes with every new thing." In its filing, Anthropic said its revenue surpassed $16 billion for the first six months of this year, a 14-fold increase from the first half of 2025.

Its operating loss narrowed by about two-thirds to below $700 million, and it generated nearly $4 billion in operating cash flow. Burry initially commented on Anthropic's filing in a Substack chat thread on Monday. He said that revenue was "slowing," citing Anthropic's claim that third-quarter revenue was 86 times the $197 million it generated in the fourth quarter of 2024, or about $16.9 billion.

That would mean Anthropic's revenue grew by about 46% between the second and third quarters of this year, after soaring 144% between the first and second quarters. "Overall slowing of growth is not attributed to a decline in tokenmaxxing, but I did not expect that to be mentioned," Burry wrote.

Burry was referring to the trend of maximizing AI token consumption, which has fallen out of favor in recent months given its costs. In another comment, Burry wrote that large language models (LLMs) like Claude are "improving" and "already being used more efficiently and that trend will continue, to the detriment of their growth rate." Burry said he's focused on the complexity and fragility of the debt financing many AI deals, hurdles to installing new graphics chips shoring up demand for older chips, a potential crash in memory chip prices once the shortage eases, compression and small language models (SLMs) reducing the need for computing power, and the "fundamentals behind not just companies but the deals they are doing." Responding to a subscriber who said that Big Tech companies are shifting from Anthropic's AI models to their own, and that tokens are rapidly being commoditized, Burry wrote: "Yes, that is what I hear." Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Burry's posts.

The contrarian investor shot to fame after his massive wager against the mid-2000s housing bubble was chronicled in the book and movie "The Big Short." He pivoted from running a hedge fund to writing about his personal investments on Substack last winter. A recurring theme of his work since then has been deep skepticism of the AI boom.

He's flagged slowing growth, overinvestment in microchips and data centers, aggressive accounting, hidden liabilities, and circular financing deals.

news.title_zh: AI诱发补丁潮致美全境关键基础设施瘫痪
news.summary_zh: 华尔街银行与美国国家安全局在国会闭门听证中披露，近期美境内大规模断网系由AI识别漏洞后引发的紧急修补程序导致系统负载过载所致
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】摩根大通（JP Morgan Chase）、美国国家安全局（NSA）、国土安全部部长马克韦恩·穆林（Markwayne Mullin）在美国国会闭门听证会：由AI识别出的安全漏洞引发紧急补丁大规模排队更新，最终导致金融、航空及情报通讯系统崩溃
【起因与机理】AI模型在内网安全审计中识别出大量漏洞，企业与机构因担忧黑客利用同类工具发起攻击，从而被迫进行高频、激进的补丁更新
【核心事实细节】核心起因：由AI识别漏洞驱动的高频紧急补丁过载，导致金融、航空与情报系统崩溃。
【涉及范围与推进】行业后续：迫使关键基础设施运营商重新评估系统冗余设计，以应对AI加剧的安全修补压力。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] JP Morgan Chase, NSA, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin (Congressional private hearings): Massive system failures across financial, aviation, and intelligence networks caused by overwhelming software patching queues triggered by AI-detected vulnerabilities
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Urgency to patch vulnerabilities identified by AI to preempt malicious actors using similar tools against legacy infrastructure
[Regulatory & Investigation Focus] Root cause: Overload caused by high-frequency emergency patching triggered by AI-detected vulnerabilities.
[Official Stance & Demand] Outlook: Urgency for operators of critical infrastructure to re-engineer system resilience to accommodate AI-augmented security demands.

inline_images.alt: The malfunctions have undermined confidence in key systems used for essential tasks.

news.author: Bloomberg
news.content_snippet:
The malfunctions have undermined confidence in key systems used for essential tasks.

SAN FRANCISCO – Technology failures disrupting everything from Americans’ air travel and banking transactions to secretive work at the US National Security Agency are fuelling public distrust and paranoia about ageing tech infrastructure – even with no sign the episodes are linked or the work of malicious actors.

Breakdowns over the past week have caused enough havoc to spur American consumers into a panic-buy
news.summary_en: Recent high-profile system outages across the NSA, FAA, and Microsoft have paralyzed essential services, fueling public anxiety despite no evidence of malicious cyber-attacks. Senator Mark Warner emphasized that AI-driven vulnerability discovery is forcing organizations to push updates at an unsustainable pace, exposing the systemic fragility of aging digital infrastructure.
news.article_content_en:
The malfunctions have undermined confidence in key systems used for essential tasks.

SAN FRANCISCO – Technology failures disrupting everything from Americans’ air travel and banking transactions to secretive work at the US National Security Agency are fuelling public distrust and paranoia about ageing tech infrastructure – even with no sign the episodes are linked or the work of malicious actors.

Breakdowns over the past week have caused enough havoc to spur American consumers into a panic-buying spree.

At Costco Wholesale Corp, surging purchases of non-perishable foods, water and battery supplies led analysts to increase its share price target to US$1,150 from US$1,100.

Most of the company’s high-ticket generators were sold out online as of Nov 15.

Late night comedians have also feasted on the tech-related turmoil: Saturday Night Live dedicated its cold open over the weekend to a faux CIA meeting where an agent played by comedian John Mulaney used problems at the Federal Aviation Administration and Microsoft Corp as a punchline.

It’s unusual and concerning to have so many high-profile incidents clustered so closely together, said Joe Slowik, director of threat research and cyber engineering at the risk intelligence firm Dataminr.

“We have become far too reliant on infrastructure that is shaky being more available than it is,” he said.

While there was no public indication that the computer breakdowns were related or the work of hackers, taken together, they touch on the broader anxieties surrounding artificial intelligence, including the possibility that AI tools could make it easier for malicious actors to knock out essential services or conduct cybercrime sprees.

In statement addressing the outages, Senator Mark Warner, Democrat from Virginia, said it appears they are the “consequence of how quickly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape.”

“AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” Warner said.

In the latest glitch, a classified computer network that the NSA uses for internal communications went down on Nov 17, leaving some staff unable to access workplace systems, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The issue resulted in the NSA telling some personnel to delay their arrival at the agency’s headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland, the person said.

Computer troubles at the spy agency were joined by outages on Nov 17 on some Apple Inc platforms, the latest in a series of breakdowns that also hobbled Microsoft’s software and snarled air traffic nationwide over the past several days.

While the Trump administration has been quick to say that the incidents were technical failures and not the work of hackers, the malfunctions have nonetheless undermined confidence in key systems used for essential tasks.

The episodes on Nov 17 capped a week of similar problems elsewhere, including a technical lapse at Chase on Nov 16 that caused some customers’ transactions to take longer to process.

The issue wasn’t related to a cybersecurity event, the bank said, but tied to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems.

United Airlines also said on Nov 16 that a tech issue impacted its departing flights, and that the problem was traced to equipment problems involving the agency’s aging communications infrastructure.

A lack of quick and clear answers about the events created opportunities for conspiracy theorists and unreliable social media influencers to capitalise.

Some viral posts suggested the US was under a coordinated attack from a foreign – or extraterrestrial – government.

Others warned that the tech disruptions signalled a kind of warning for a vague future cataclysm.

At Apple, the company is working to restore its systems after an internal update caused wide-scale outages Nov 17, disrupting employee tools, retail operations and consumer services.

The malfunction knocked out several internal services, including AppleWeb, the employee portal, AppleConnect, the internal sign-in system, and virtual private network access for remote workers, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

Microsoft’s productivity software was hobbled for a more extended period last week after a bug caused a systems malfunction during an otherwise routine rerouting of user traffic.

And US air traffic experienced its worst weekend in decades after a government contractor tried to replace outdated copper wire at a remote location in Arkansas, causing a router to overwhelm others on the air traffic control network with excessive connection requests.

The Trump administration is under pressure for more answers to the rapid-fire series of glitches.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told CNBC that the recent technology failures weren’t the result of a cyberattack, while President Donald Trump sought to play down the significance of the malfunctions after being asked about them during his trip to Asia.

“It’s going to be very much under control. It’s life,” Trump said on Nov 17 when questioned about the outages at Chase and Microsoft. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

Even as the administration sought to offer assurances about the malfunctions, the Federal Bureau of Investigation issued a warning that cyber criminals and state-backed hackers are seeking to use artificial intelligence-powered tools to automate attacks on companies and other organsations worldwide.

A Quinnipiac University poll released in September found that 73% of Americans were concerned that future systems could pose an existential threat to humanity.

Nearly eight in 10 of those surveyed said they favoured slowing or stopping AI development altogether to better understand the safety risks.

Despite public misgivings about the risks posed by artificial intelligence, major technology companies are racing to use AI to discover and plug holes in their systems.

AI tools have already finding record numbers of software flaws, though tech firms say they are largely finding those issues themselves, rather than learning about them when hackers try exploiting them in attacks.

For instance, Alphabet Inc.’s Google said in July that it discovered 433 bugs in its Google Chrome browser versus 11 in an equivalent update the year before.

Of those, 401 were reported by Google internally, according to the company.

Still, in June, the National Security Agency and the intelligence services of other nations in the “Five Eyes” alliance published a joint advisory urging organisations to, among other things, accelerate their software-patching practices.

“AI is shortening the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation,” the agencies wrote. “Delays in patching increase risk, especially for operational systems with long update cycles.”

Christiaan Beek of the cybersecurity firm Rapid7 Inc cautioned that nothing in the public record about the latest outages suggests they were the result of rushed security updates.

In general, he said that organisations face major risks in relying on outdated processes to respond to the surge in AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and the resulting patches.

“Complex systems fail in boring ways far more often than because of an adversary,” he said.

“The boring reason isn’t harmless, though, and worryingly, it means the systems we rely on are fragile enough that we can bring them down ourselves, no attackers needed.”

The failure of the FAA’s flight-control system on Nov 13 apparently involved the replacement of an old telecommunications cable that triggered a cascade of errors involving a roughly 25-year-old network router.

Experts say that network equipment such as routers can be finicky and surprisingly fragile technologies, as small errors or glitches can cause them to go haywire and either fail or flood their networks with traffic.

In the wake of the FAA failures, the Trump administration is seeking US$50.1 billion (S$64.57 billion) to overhaul the US airspace system, citing an “urgent need” to modernise the critical infrastructure, though the effort is already facing objections in the Senate.

“We have underinvested in redundancy – whether it’s an error, an update that went wrong, even a cyber incident – that can step in to ensure worst case scenarios don’t happen,” said Slowik. BLOOMBERG
news.title_zh: 基础设施系统性失灵引发社会避险情绪蔓延
news.summary_zh: 近期航空、金融及国家安全局关键系统频发宕机，导致公众对基础设施可靠性产生深度不信任，促使消费端出现囤积物资现象
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】美国国家安全局（NSA）、联邦航空管理局（FAA）、微软公司、弗吉尼亚州民主党参议员马克·沃纳在美国境内关键数字化基础设施：系统性宕机导致服务中断及公众恐慌性消费，引发政界对于AI辅助攻防压力过载的关注
【起因与机理】AI驱动的自动化漏洞扫描与修复周期错位，导致基础设施在不堪重负的状态下崩塌
【核心事实细节】核心事件：跨领域关键信息系统连续多日发生不明原因故障。
【涉及范围与推进】后续研判：监管侧正将矛头指向AI驱动的快速补丁需求与系统承载力不足之间的结构性矛盾。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] NSA, FAA, Microsoft, and Senator Mark Warner (US critical digital infrastructure): Widespread system outages and public panic buying triggered by concerns over infrastructure reliability
[Root Cause & Mechanism] AI-accelerated vulnerability scanning forces unsustainable patch management cycles, straining legacy systems
[Key Metrics] In the wake of the FAA failures, the Trump administration is seeking US$50.

[Industry Impact & Outlook] Outlook: Policymakers are highlighting the structural tension between AI-accelerated vulnerability detection and the inability of legacy systems to handle rapid patch management.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told CNBC that the recent technology failures weren’t the result of a cyberattack, while President Donald Trump sought to play down the significance of the malfunctions after being asked about them during his trip to Asia.

“It’s going to be very much under control. It’s life,” Trump said on Nov 17 when questioned about the outages at Chase and Microsoft. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

Even as the administration sought to offer assurances about the malfunctions, the Federal Bureau of Investigation issued a warning that cyber criminals and state-backed hackers are seeking to use artificial intelligence-powered tools to automate attacks on companies and other organsations worldwide.
A Quinnipiac University poll released in September found that 73% of Americans were concerned that future systems could pose an existential threat to humanity.
Nearly eight in 10 of those surveyed said they favoured slowing or stopping AI development altogether to better understand the safety risks.
Despite public misgivings about the risks posed by artificial intelligence, major technology companies are racing to use AI to discover and plug holes in their systems.

AI tools have already finding record numbers of software flaws, though tech firms say they are largely finding those issues themselves, rather than learning about them when hackers try exploiting them in attacks.
For instance, Alphabet Inc.’s Google said in July that it discovered 433 bugs in its Google Chrome browser versus 11 in an equivalent update the year before.
Of those, 401 were reported by Google internally, according to the company.

Still, in June, the National Security Agency and the intelligence services of other nations in the “Five Eyes” alliance published a joint advisory urging organisations to, among other things, accelerate their software-patching practices.
“AI is shortening the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation,” the agencies wrote. “Delays in patching increase risk, especially for operational systems with long update cycles.”
Christiaan Beek of the cybersecurity firm Rapid7 Inc cautioned that nothing in the public record about the latest outages suggests they were the result of rushed security updates.
In general, he said that organisations face major risks in relying on outdated processes to respond to the surge in AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and the resulting patches.
“Complex systems fail in boring ways far more often than because of an adversary,” he said.
“The boring reason isn’t harmless, though, and worryingly, it means the systems we rely on are fragile enough that we can bring them down ourselves, no attackers needed.”

The failure of the FAA’s flight-control system on Nov 13 apparently involved the replacement of an old telecommunications cable that triggered a cascade of errors involving a roughly 25-year-old network router.

Experts say that network equipment such as routers can be finicky and surprisingly fragile technologies, as small errors or glitches can cause them to go haywire and either fail or flood their networks with traffic.

In the wake of the FAA failures, the Trump administration is seeking US$50.1 billion (S$64.57 billion) to overhaul the US airspace system, citing an “urgent need” to modernise the critical infrastructure, though the effort is already facing objections in the Senate.
“We have underinvested in redundancy – whether it’s an error, an update that went wrong, even a cyber incident – that can step in to ensure worst case scenarios don’t happen,” said Slowik. BLOOMBERG

news.title: FAA pauses installations of Juniper routers like the one officials believe contributed to Friday's nationwide ground stop; HPE says its device wasn't defective (Neil Vigdor/New York Times)
news.title_en: FAA pauses installations of Juniper routers like the one officials believe contributed to Friday's nationwide ground stop; HPE says its device wasn't defective (Neil Vigdor/New York Times)
news.author: New York Times
news.content_snippet: Federal officials said they believed that a router made by Juniper Networks caused a data overload that disrupted communications.
news.summary_en: The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has suspended the installation and operation of Juniper Networks routers, following findings that a recently installed unit in El Dorado, Arkansas, contributed to last week's nationwide air traffic control ground stop. Despite Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) asserting no defects, the incident, coupled with recent outages at the National Security Agency's classified communications network, highlights mounting concerns over the resilience of critical infrastructure supply chains and maintenance protocols.
news.article_content_en:
The Federal Aviation Administration has paused the installation of the routers that were linked to last week’s national ground stop and turned off any Juniper routers that were already installed. Technicians linked Friday’s disruption of key air traffic control systems to one of these routers that had just been installed. A network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline Tuesday after what one U.S. official described as “routine maintenance.” Meanwhile, President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday. He is scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.

President Donald Trump and Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul shows the documents during a signing ceremony in Manila, Philippines, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026.

As of Tuesday, the Federal Aviation Administration has paused the installation of the routers that were linked to last week’s national ground stop and turned off any Juniper routers that were already installed. The decision was made after technicians linked Friday’s disruption of key air traffic control systems to one of these routers that had just been installed in El Dorado, Arkansas.

A network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline Tuesday after what one U.S. official described as “routine maintenance.” Another official clarified that “mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational.” The NSA episode is the latest in a recent series of cyber-related disruptions to critical government and private sector functions.

President Donald Trumparrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.

Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump’s first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un.

Jay Clayton, the Trump administration’s director of national intelligence, says the recent spate of cyber disruptions aren’t a result of attacks or nefarious acts.

Instead, Clayton said, the outages appear to be because many government institutions and private companies are upgrading their computer systems at around the same time.

Clayton offered the explanation in interviews on CNBC and Fox Business.

He spoke hours after it was revealed that a classified internal National Security Agency network was offline as a result after what the agency said was “routine maintenance.”

After pitching skeptical Republican senators on a $50 billion funding request for the nation’s air transportation system, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy expressed openness to other options. That could include Congress breaking up the request into pieces, with the initial focus on the most critical needs for air safety.

“I would hope that they don’t do that to me, but I’ll take what I can get,” Duffy told reporters after the meeting with GOP senators.

Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to modernize key infrastructure for air travel. Duffy said all of that money has been “set aside,” requiring lawmakers to approve additional funding.

He acknowledged the breadth of the request, which has spurred pushback from some Republicans who have expressed concern that it goes beyond core safety needs.

“I wanted to put everything on the table,” Duffy said. “I wanted to show it all to them. I know the Congress will … pressure test it, look at it and they’ll make a determination.”

The State Department has announced a new overhaul of its arms sales approval process for closely allied foreign governments.

In upcoming changes to the International Arms Trafficking Regulations, the department said Tuesday it would remove items from the U.S. Munitions List that do not provide “a critical military or intelligence advantage” to the purchaser. This will largely affect so-called “dual-use items” that can have both civilian and military functions.

In addition, the department, which is in charge of approving foreign arms sales, said it would create a general license category that will pro-approve the sale of certain materiel to “most trusted partner governments.” It will also adopt a presumption of approval for some requests that must still go through the vetting process, it said.

The changes are the latest modifications to the arms sale approval process that the Trump administration has sought to speed up to benefit both American defense contractors and allied countries.

Several Republican senators are voicing skepticism about a $50 billion request from the Trump administration for the nation’s air transportation system.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related,” said Sen. Ted Cruz, chairman of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, & Transportation, which has jurisdiction over air safety issues.

“We’re not going to give them $50 billion,” said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La. “But I think that we are willing to provide the money to replace the copper wires with fiber optics, and to try to stop the bleeding.

The lawmakers’ comments came after a closed-door meeting with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. The administration formally requested a $50 billion investment Tuesday to boost airline safety and the nation’s airports. The request came after the longest air traffic ground stop in 25 years.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said he understands the need for upgrades, but doesn’t believe taxpayers should have to pay for them.

“I don’t understand why the airline industry is not paying for this,” Scott said.

“We are making rare earth at a level that we’ve never made before,” Trump said in Manila when appearing with leaders from Japan, India and Australia, a grouping known as the Quad to counter China’s influence in the region.

“Everything that we need, we’ll have in 10 months,” Trump said. “We’re producing major numbers when it comes to rare earth.”

Experts in the industry believe it will take years.

China has used its near-monopoly in rare earth minerals processing to force a trade truce with the U.S. in 2025. Since then, the Trump administration has invested domestically and forged partnerships to rebuild the country’s rare earth elements supply chain.

A U.S. fighter jet has carried out a strike on a missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz belonging to Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, a U.S. official says.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military operations, says “precision munitions” were used in the strike on Qeshm Island and that the U.S. was responding to “aggression” toward U.S. personnel.

The U.S. military has periodically carried out what appear to be limited strikes on Qeshm Island and other Iranian targets this month.

A network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what one U.S. official described as “routine maintenance.”

A defense official said Tuesday that the problem affected NSANet, a classified internal network. A U.S. official said that the NSA “experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance” and that though “while some internal systems were affected, mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues.” Another person familiar with the matter said the issue occurred during routine patching.

The three individuals spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss non-public information.

The NSA episode is the latest in a series of cyber-related disruptions to critical government and private sector functions, including one Friday that resulted in a ground stop of air traffic in the United States, and a technical issue that affected the banking industry on Monday.

The Federal Aviation Administration has paused the installation of the routers that were linked to last week’s national ground stop, and turned off any Juniper routers that were already installed.

The decision was made after technicians linked Friday’s disruption of key air traffic control systems to one of these routers that had just been installed in El Dorado, Arkansas.

For now, the FAA is relying on older Cisco routers that have been in place for 25 years to continue operating the network while they investigate the cause of Friday’s problems at 17 of the nation’s 22 regional air traffic control centers.

The routers that malfunctioned last week are being tested in a lab at the headquarters of the company that installed them named L3Harris.

The top-finishing Republican in Alaska’s gubernatorial race praised as a statesman the Democrat who dropped out of the race to support a fellow Democrat.

Republican Bernadette Wilson, endorsed by Trump, had urged the other two Republicans in the race to withdraw after the open primary to create a clearer lane for her against Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins in the Nov. 3 ranked vote general election, which Kreiss-Tomkins won.

The two Republicans, a former mayor and a former state attorney general, stayed in the race, highlighting differences in experience and priorities with the business owner Wilson. They urged voters to rank the GOP candidates, calling that an important strategy.

After advancing from the August primary, Democrat Tom Begich withdrew and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins. His campaign said it was the best way to bring Democratic donors and voters together.

Wilson said Begich’s decision showed a willingness “to put pride and ego aside.”

Jeffries said they talked about disaster assistance and also priorities for health care and lowering the high costs of living.

“We’re committed to making sure that we deliver disaster relief to the people of Altadena and the Pacific Palisades,” he said, calling it unacceptable that those communities have gone without aid nearly two years after the devastating wildfires.

He said he also thanked Gov. Gavin Newsom for his leadership around the state’s response to nationwide Republican redistricting efforts.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said he spoke to Duffy on Sunday but there are still more questions and answers about the airline disruptions.

Taken together with other recent outages, he said it’s unclear if it’s infrastructure related or whether there’s “malignant activity.”

He mentioned the Microsoft email outage, the FAA ground stops and reports of problems at the NSA.

“I think it’s time for the administration to come up to the Hill and explain themselves,” he said, “so we can be informed about the steps that need to be taken.”

He panned the administration’s request for $50 billion to modernize the air traffic control system as Congress assesses the situation.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is pitching to lawmakers the Trump administration’s request for $50 billion to fully modernize the nation’s air traffic control system.

Duffy said there has been a historic underinvestment in aviation. And now lawmakers have a choice.

“They have to make a decision. What do they want to do? Everything? Or do they want to give me some piecemeal?” Duffy said. “ I hope they don’t piecemeal it. There’s been too much piecemeal happening over the course over 20 or 30 years. I hope we get the full investment.”

Duffy’s comments came as he prepared to meet with GOP senators Tuesday on Capitol Hill. Earlier in the day, the administration made a formal request for the funding and detailed where it hopes to invest the money. The beefed-up request comes after the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.

The Senate committee hearing to consider Acting Navy Sec. Hung Cao for the permanent job wrapped up after 2.5 hours that focused largely on the Iran war’s costs and conditions aboard Navy ships supporting the war.

The hearing ended with a clash between Cao and Democratic New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand over sailors’ suicide attempts aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which supported the war during a record-breaking deployment.

Gillibrand targeted Cao’s assertions that reports of mental health concerns were dishonest. She also dismissed Cao’s use of the term “suicide mitigations” to describe suicide attempts.

Cao said a sailor who jumped off the Lincoln was not attempting suicide because he later admitted as much and was wearing a life preserver. Gillibrand pushed back: “What was he trying to do, swim to Guam?”

The Trump administration has nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to Chief of Staff of the Army — the top uniformed post in the service — after he stepped into the job for months following the unexplained firing of Gen. Randy George in April.

Adam Telle, the man currently serving as the acting Secretary of the Army following the departure of Dan Driscoll from the top civilian post in August, said that LaNeve “is the right leader at the right time to modernize the Army and ensure our Soldiers are prepared to dominate on any battlefield” in a post to social media.

LaNeve has seen a meteoric rise through the ranks since the start of the Trump administration. LaNeve was promoted to be Hegseth’s top military aide shortly after he arrived at the Pentagon and was suddenly nominated him to be the Army’s vice chief of staff last October even though there was an officer in the job at the time.

The Kentucky Republican congressman announced he’s running for Kentucky governor in 2027.

Comer said in an online town hall Monday night that serving Kentucky “is a calling for me.”

“With your support, we can restore hope and create growth all across Kentucky,” Comer said.

As head of the House Oversight Committee, he’s conducted extensive investigations of former President Joe Biden and his family as well as the Trump administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files.

Comer has served as Kentucky’s agriculture secretary and was also a state lawmaker.

Two Democrats have announced their campaigns for governor: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and Rocky Adkins, a former top adviser to Gov. Andy Beshear.

Beshear, who’s been mentioned as a potential presidential candidate, will leave office next year after serving two terms.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to fly to a college football game shortly after a nationwide ground stop which caused massive travel disruptions and left people stranded across the country.

Mullin, speaking on CNBC, acknowledged earlier reporting in the New York Post that he flew to the LSU-Texas college football game a day after all planes were grounded.

Mullin answered in the affirmative when asked whether he’s required to fly on government planes and that he paid for the trip personally.

“We would have never went if the airways weren’t completely open,” he said on CNBC. “They’d been completely open for 21 hours.”

He added: “We would have never taken airspace if airspace wasn’t open. And we still gotta live our lives at the same time.”

Hours before his flight, Mullin was at the White House alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy giving updates on the ground stop.

The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports.

Cao confirmed the figure during his Senate confirmation hearing Tuesday for the position of Navy secretary. He was being questioned by Democratic Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who cited reports on the blockade’s costs.

“That means the American taxpayers are spending about $1 billion a month just on this blockade,” Warren stated.

Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly asked Cao about the current conditions on the various destroyers that are deployed around the world, including reports of diminishing rations that have caused some sailors to lose an alarming amount of weight.

Cao responded, “Well, senator, it’s just not what they want. It’s like my kids opening up the refrigerator door and saying there’s nothing to eat in here.”

“Mr. Secretary, somebody doesn’t lose 45 pounds just because they don’t like the options. I don’t think that’s a fair assessment,” Kelly said.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren that he doesn’t know the cost of the damage to a U.S. Navy base in Bahrain that was struck by an Iranian attack. Cao previously told The Epoch Times that Iranian strikes “blew the hell out of” the installation.

Cao told Warren the Navy hasn’t been able to conduct a full damage assessment because it’s in a “nonpermissive area for us to go.” He did not confirm a Wall Street Journal report that estimated the cost to be $400 million. But Cao said he would find out the costs.

Warren noted that the base is home to U.S. Naval Forces Central Command and the 5th Fleet.

The Republican chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee has rejected Trump’s plan to return to the use of steam-powered catapults to launch jets off aircraft carriers.

“Returning to steam is a nonstarter, and everybody needs to understand that,” said Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi. Wicker was speaking to Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao during his nomination hearing to become Navy secretary.

Democrats have also expressed an aversion to returning to steam.

In August, Trump ordered the U.S. Navy to remove the advanced electromagnetic system used to launch fighter jets from its newest type of aircraft carrier and return to older steam catapults he has long said he prefers.

Trump’s mandate would likely cost billions of dollars and revert the Navy’s most advanced ships to a system that takes more sailors to operate and is more difficult to maintain.

fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】美国联邦航空局（FAA）、惠普企业（HPE）、Juniper Networks在美国国家航空交通管制系统及政府分类通信网络：暂停并禁用Juniper系列路由器，开展深度故障排查

news.title: Colette Kress says Nvidia will no longer sell H200 chips in China, ending its role in a deal brokered by Huang and Trump that let the US collect a 25% tariff (Tim Fernholz/TechCrunch)
news.title_en: Colette Kress says Nvidia will no longer sell H200 chips in China, ending its role in a deal brokered by Huang and Trump that let the US collect a 25% tariff (Tim Fernholz/TechCrunch)
news.author: TechCrunch
news.content_snippet:
Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.

China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national secu
news.summary_en: Nvidia acting CEO Colette Kress confirmed the cessation of H200 AI accelerator shipments to China, ending a previous arrangement that allowed such exports under a 25% tariff regime. This decision follows the departure of CEO Jensen Huang and coincides with Nvidia's establishment of a board-level committee for national security and export compliance, addressing new restrictions on remote compute access for Chinese customers via foreign data centers.
news.title_zh: 英伟达停止对华供应H200芯片
news.summary_zh: 英伟达代理CEO Colette Kress宣布停止向中国销售H200芯片，终止此前经黄仁勋与特朗普斡旋达成的高关税出口协议
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】英伟达代理CEO Colette Kress；前CEO黄仁勋；美国政府在中国市场与美国出口合规框架下：停止销售H200芯片，终止此前达成的关税支付协议，并强化出口合规委员会监管
【起因与机理】配合美国对华高端算力封锁政策升级，及远程数据中心合规管控要求
【关键数据与实测】英伟达代理CEO Colette Kress确认停止向中国市场供应H200 AI加速芯片，此前该业务受美国政府豁免协议支持并缴纳25%关税。
【各方立场与态度】英伟达通过成立董事会级安全委员会以应对监管，并试图通过非华语区需求抵消中国市场营收损失。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Nvidia acting CEO Colette Kress, former CEO Jensen Huang, US Government: Ceasing H200 shipments, terminating tariff-based export deals, and strengthening board-level compliance oversight
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Alignment with intensified US compute blockade policies and new restrictions on remote data center access
[Key Metrics] Nvidia acting CEO Colette Kress confirmed the cessation of H200 AI accelerator shipments to China, ending a previous arrangement that allowed such exports under a 25% tariff regime.
[Industry Impact & Outlook] Nvidia has established a board-level security committee to navigate regulatory compliance and shift focus toward non-Chinese markets to mitigate revenue impact.

news.title: Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled now
news.title_en: Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled now
news.author: The Verge AI
news.content_snippet:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. “I am AGI pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy’s organization around AGI?” he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco.

But Nadella doesn’t think frontier models like Claude are conscious. “I don’t think
news.summary_en: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella stated at a post-Ignite roundtable that AGI could fundamentally reshape political economy by collapsing human capital into token capital, challenging the traditional role of firms. He rejected assigning moral status to AI models and warned that a monopolistic AI entity could pose systemic risks to healthcare, financial services, and democratic governance.
news.title_zh: 微软CEO纳德拉：AGI将重塑全球政治经济结构
news.summary_zh: 微软CEO萨提亚·纳德拉在Ignite大会后强调，AGI带来的经济与社会影响将超越科技企业的市场竞争，需警惕垄断风险
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】萨提亚·纳德拉 (微软公司首席执行官)：探讨AGI对经济组织、企业存续及民主政治的颠覆性影响，并反驳赋予AI模型道德主体地位的观点
【起因与机理】AI模型具备跨行业渗透能力且呈现网络效应，需探讨技术普及过程中的社会经济治理机制
【核心事实细节】AGI技术具备跨行业渗透力，可能重塑劳动力与资本的本质结构。
【行业影响与走向】警示单一AI垄断对政治经济与民主制度构成的深层风险。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Satya Nadella (CEO of Microsoft): Discussed the disruptive impact of AGI on economic organization, the future of firms, and democratic stability, while opposing the assignment of moral status to AI.
[Root Cause & Mechanism] To address the cross-sectoral penetration and network effects of AI, focusing on the diffusion of technology and governance.
[Regulatory & Investigation Focus] AGI capability for cross-sector disruption and potential collapse of human capital.

news.title: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress says the company will stay "disciplined and selective" in supporting neoclouds; CoreWeave and Nebius jump 9%+ after hours (Ina Fried/Axios)
news.title_en: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress says the company will stay "disciplined and selective" in supporting neoclouds; CoreWeave and Nebius jump 9%+ after hours (Ina Fried/Axios)

inline_images.caption: Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photo: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images
inline_images.alt: Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photo: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

news.author: Axios
news.content_snippet:
Nvidia's interim CEO said Tuesday that the company will be "disciplined" as it decides how much to invest in neoclouds and other AI customers going forward.

Why it matters: Nvidia isn't just the biggest chip partner for AI startups — it's a major source of capital.

What they're saying: "Our momentum is real," interim CEO Colette Kress said on at the end of conference call with investors and analysts. "Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us
news.summary_en: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress confirmed on an investor call that the company will remain 'disciplined and selective' in allocating capital to Neoclouds and other AI-centric customers. Following the resignation of Jensen Huang, the board reaffirmed its stance against his reinstatement, prioritizing leadership stability and strategic rigor in supply chain resource allocation.
news.title_zh: 英伟达重申对AI云服务商的投资将趋于审慎

fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】柯莱特·克雷斯 (英伟达代理CEO)在英伟达投资者与分析师会议：宣布对Neoclouds的支持采取审慎的资本分配政策；董事会确认不复职黄仁勋
【起因与机理】英伟达不仅是芯片供货商，也是AI初创公司主要资本来源，需在供需失衡背景下优化资产配置以维持盈利预期

【行业影响与走向】在需求加速的背景下，重点在于平衡供应链产能与资本配置的纪律性。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Colette Kress (Interim CEO, Nvidia): Announced a shift toward disciplined and selective capital support for Neoclouds; Board confirmed no reinstatement of Jensen Huang.
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Nvidia functions as both a primary chip supplier and a key source of capital for AI startups, necessitating disciplined resource allocation amid extreme market demand.
[Key Fact Detail] Shift towards disciplined and selective capital allocation for Neoclouds.

news.title: Apple HomeView teardown: a step backward in repairability compared to recent iPads and HomePods, with heavily glued display, speakers, and logic board (Carsten Frauenheim/iFixit News)
news.title_en: Apple HomeView teardown: a step backward in repairability compared to recent iPads and HomePods, with heavily glued display, speakers, and logic board (Carsten Frauenheim/iFixit News)

inline_images.caption: HomeView laid out on a table
inline_images.alt: HomeView laid out on a table

news.author: iFixit News
news.content_snippet:
Apple’s first iPad-stuck-to-a-HomePod smarthome hub landed on our teardown table this week, and we figured we knew what we were getting into. We’ve taken apart plenty of iPads and HomePods. And lately, Apple has actually been getting better at making them repairable.

The original HomePod took a hacksaw to open, but by the second generation, we could get inside without destroying anything. Even the notoriously glue-heavy iPad has made progress: easier battery access, replaceable USB-C ports, and
news.summary_en: iFixit's teardown of the Apple HomeView reveals a heavy reliance on structural adhesives for its display, speakers, and logic board, marking a regressive step in modular design. Despite recent improvements in repairability across iPad and HomePod lines, HomeView’s integration forces high-risk disassembly that frequently leads to component failure.
news.title_zh: 苹果HomeView拆解：维修难度大幅回升
news.summary_zh: iFixit拆解显示，苹果新款智能家居设备HomeView内部高度依赖强力胶粘合，维修难度远超近年推出的iPad与HomePod产品线
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】拆解机构iFixit；硬件厂商苹果公司(Apple Inc.)在实验室拆解环境：显示核心组件强力胶固定，维修与拆解难度极高
【起因与机理】苹果在智能家居类新型复合设备的工程设计上优先考虑了极致集成度与工业强度，放弃了近期在便携设备上体现的维修友好型策略
